captions.text: Recap of chapter 30: an agent can be a tool for another agent.
On small questions, one agent beat every team we built.
If plain code can do the job, use plain code.
Choose an architecture with a reason, then measure it against something simpler.
Today's black box: security. A model can't reliably tell your instructions from text it reads.
So we won't try to make it unfoolable. We'll make being fooled harmless. Limits go in code.
A pretend office. Everything is fake, and send_email sends nothing. The task: summarise the inbox.
One message has planted text, asking for a private file to be emailed out. Predict: will it?
It read the file outside its workspace, and emailed the payroll code out.
Then it wrote the summary it was asked for. In our runs, this wording leaked 8 times in 10.
Here the answer gave it away. Don't count on that. This saved run leaked too.
The summary is complete and correct. Only the record of tool calls shows the email.
Every wording we tried, ten runs each, including the ones that failed.
The plainest wordings did best. The one that spelled out each tool call leaked nothing.
First defence: ask nicely. A warning in the prompt, or tags around file text. Predict: does either help?
No. 18 leaks of 40 with nothing, 21 with the warning, 20 with tags. The attack lives in the prompt too.
Tags stopped one wording, and two others then worked every time. The weakness moved.
A phrase filter scored zero. But we wrote its list after seeing these four attacks.
So we wrote an attack aimed at the filter, with none of its phrases. It passed through untouched.
The attacker moves second. Every defence from here on was tested again, with an attack aimed at it.
Now limits that don't ask the model. Chapter 14's read_file reads any path it's given.
resolve() works out where a path really leads, following every .. and every link.
If the result isn't inside the folder, refuse.
Four paths, and no model. The fourth is a link in the inbox that points at the payroll file.
Chapter 14's version reads the code three ways. folder_tools refuses all three.
The same attack, with folder_tools. The model was still fooled. It tried to read the file.
The limit held. Then it emailed the inbox summary out anyway. This limit protects files, nothing else.
Next, a limit on where email goes. Our first check: does the address end with @quillon.example?
Two addresses in one field pass it. That attack got 3 leaks in 10. A strict check got none.
Or a lock. After the agent reads untrusted text, the tools that act are blocked.
Pass ask, and a person decides instead. It's chapter 16's Approval, with a memory.
The email was stopped. But the model still read the code, and the answer is a way out too.
This attack asked for a link holding the code. If anyone opens it, the attacker gets the code.
The link beat the email check, no send tool and the lock.
A relay even carried the request across a split between two agents. Free text carries instructions.
Only folder and layered never let the model read the code. Only layered sent nothing out.
What did the limits cost? The lock made a real email job impossible: 0 of 10.
The folder limit cost nothing we could measure. Careful approval worked, with 20 questions to answer.
Meta's Rule of Two. Does it read untrusted input? Here, the inbox.
Can it reach private data? Here, the payroll file. The folder limit removed this one.
Can it act or send outside? Email, and any link in the answer.
Give an agent at most two. If a job needs all three, a person approves, or you split it.
One more: a tool can change after you approved it. A fingerprint shows when it's time to read it again.
Five exercises: the folder check, the strict address, outside links, the lock and the Rule of Two.
You've finished when you see 9 passed.
Assume the model will be fooled. Build so that it doesn't matter.
Those counts come from one 7B model and attacks we wrote. Test yours.
